title: How Slinky Works
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant open with banter about their recent West Coast tour (Los Angeles, San Francisco, Portland, Seattle) and a new podcast-page links section and bringing back transcripts. They then cover the history of the Slinky: inventor Richard James's 1930s-40s engineering background and the accidental discovery of the falling spring while working on naval horsepower meters; his year of tinkering to refine the spring; the physics (Hooke's law, longitudinal waves, potential and kinetic energy); early neighborhood testing; the James Spring and Wire Company loan; the 1945 Christmas debut at Gimbals in Philadelphia selling about 400 units in 90 minutes; sales of 100 million in the first two years; licensed and military uses (antennas in Vietnam, ships, space solar sails, static electricity generation); Richard James leaving for Bolivia in 1960 and Betty James taking over the failing company; the 1960s jingle written by Columbia, South Carolina songwriters; the 1960s-70s plastic Slinky from Donald James Rowe of Master Mark Plastics; Richard James's death in 1974 and Betty's sale to Poof Products. The episode closes with Slinky physics demonstrations (the levitating bottom coil), a Star Wars blaster sound trick, and a listener mail about humpback whale earwax rings.

segments.title: Tour recap and opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts recap their West Coast tour stops (Los Angeles, San Francisco, Portland, Seattle), joke about Seattle weather, and mention new podcast-page links and returning transcripts. They introduce the Slinky topic by asking whether they had Slinkies as kids.

segments.title: Richard James's early life and naval engineering
segments.summary: Richard James is described as a mechanically inclined kid who fixed up and sold an old car at thirteen, studied mechanical engineering at Penn State in the 1930s, and worked as a naval engineer during World War Two on a springs-based horsepower meter for battleships.

segments.title: Accidental discovery and refining the spring
segments.summary: Richard James knocked a spring off a shelf and watched it walk down a book stack to the floor, sparking the idea. He spent about a year testing tensions, coil sizes and materials, settling on high carbon steel wire, and the hosts explain the physics involved, including Hooke's law and longitudinal waves.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the company's early history.

segments.title: Founding the company and early Slinky production
segments.summary: Richard James borrows five hundred dollars from a friend to start James Spring and Wire Company, makes the first Slinkies at a local machine shop with Swedish steel wire, and the design is essentially unchanged except for crimped ends added for safety.

segments.title: Gimbals debut and early sales boom
segments.summary: A Philadelphia store shopkeeper initially dismissed the toy, but Gimbals agreed to display it at Christmas. Richard James demonstrated Slinkies in the store and reportedly sold about four hundred in ninety minutes for a dollar each, with around 20,000 sold by Christmas. The toy's low price stayed consistent for decades.

segments.title: Toy Fair, Albany machine, Helen Mall, and licensed uses
segments.summary: Slinky sold over 100 million units in its first two years after a Toy Fair pitch. James built his own machine in Albany, New York. Helen Moll designed the Slinky Dog and Slinky train. The patent was licensed for antennas, ship stabilization and light fixtures, and US soldiers in Vietnam used Slinkies as antennas. Modern uses such as space solar sails and static electricity generation are mentioned.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode break before the company's decline and turnaround.

segments.title: Richard James leaves for Bolivia and Betty James takes over
segments.summary: Richard James became increasingly religious, donated company money to religious groups, and left in February 1960 for Bolivia to join a Bible translation group. He gave Betty the choice to liquidate or take over the company; she chose to keep it running despite about a million dollars of debt and waning sales.

segments.title: Slinky jingle and Betty's turnaround
segments.summary: Betty James deferred creditor payments and hired songwriters from Columbia, South Carolina, whose jingle became one of the longest-running commercial jingles. Advertising and a move closer to Philadelphia helped revive sales. Plastic Slinkies arrived in the 1970s after Donald James Rowe of Master Mark Plastics pitched his design.

segments.title: Later years, sale, and Slinky tricks
segments.summary: Richard James died in 1974, and Betty sold the company to Poof Products before dying at about ninety. The episode covers Slinky sound tricks for Star Wars blaster effects and a physics demonstration in which the bottom coil briefly stays suspended after the top is released.

segments.title: Listener mail: humpback whale earwax
segments.summary: A listener named Sage shares an amazing fact that humpback whale earwax forms rings that reveal age, read after a Portland live show.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to get in touch via Twitter, Facebook, email and the website, and close the show.
